utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning to you all. My apologies for having kept everybody waiting due to a logistical problem. So why don't we begin. If the witness kindly take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Besic. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Examination by Gaynor:

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, could you state your fall name, please?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: My same is Sead Besic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I'm working at the canton Sarajevo MUP. I'm criminal technician, I'm junior inspector. That is my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You previously testified in the trials of Stanislav Galic, Dragomir Milosevic, and Momcilo Perisic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Previously provided statements to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And you've had an opportunity, I believe, to review an amalgamated statement containing relevant portions of your previous testimonies and statements; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask the Registrar to bring up 65 ter 22060, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In front of you, Mr. Besic, do you see the first page of your amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Does the amalgamated statement accurately reflect the evidence you have previously given, and if you were examined on the same topics today, would you provide the same information to the Court?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to seek admission of the amalgamated statements, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1966, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll now read a short summary of the statement of Mr. Besic. Mr. Besic was -- Mr. Besic was a criminal technician in the CSB Sarajevo of the RBiH MUP. He participated in investigations of shelling and sniping incidents in Sarajevo. Mr. Besic's duties involved preparing diagrams and photographs of crime scenes and retrieving physical evidence. His statement concerns investigations into the shelling of a residential area in Dobrinja on the 4th of February, 1994. The shelling of the Markale Market on the 5th of February 1994, and on the 28th of August, 1995, and the sniping incident on the 18th of November, 1994. In respect of the Markale incident on the 4th of February, 1994, Markale I in which 66 people were killed and over 140 were wounded, Mr. Besic states that during the initial examination of the impact point, the stabiliser could not be seen above ground level. Mr. Besic participated in cleaning the area around the impact point. The stabiliser was subsequently removed by French UNPROFOR personnel and later provided to Mr. Besic. Mr. Besic confirms that scene, including part of the work by a member of UNPROFOR, to remove the stabiliser was recorded by one of his colleagues using a video camera. Mr. Besic also participated in the investigation of the shelling of the Markale Market on the 28th of August, 1995, Markale II, which killed 43 people and injured 75. Mr. Besic took a number of photographs and prepared a diagram of the incident scene. Mr. Besic also participated in an investigation of a scheduled sniping incident on the 18th of November, 1994, in which Dzenana Sokolovic and her son Nermin Divovic were fired on while walking on Zmaja Od Bosne. Dzenana Sokolovic was wounded and her son was killed. At the time of the incident, they had been walking home from Frazno where -- pardon me, that's Hrasno, where they had gone to collect firewood the previous day. Mr. Besic's tasks were to photograph and to make a diagram of the scene. That concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Besic, my questions to you today will only concern the Markale I incident and the Markale II incident. Starting with Markale I, I'd like to call up a video which has been admitted as P1711. If we could play that video, please. We are going to play from the start until 11 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Besic, could you describe the scene that you've just seen on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is Markale I market. On the photograph, you can see the damage, the stalls turned over, and on the photograph you can also see me, the person that you can see on the photograph is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we can now go to 2 minutes and 33 seconds, please. If we could play that for a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, if we could stop there, please. What we've stopped now at 2 minutes and 38 seconds. What did you see in that portion of the video, Mr. Besic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: This is the centre of the mortar shell explosion where you can see material that has fallen on to this place. By cleaning it, you can see much better, the centre of the explosion of the mortar projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was it your standard practice to clean the area around the impact of a mortar projectile during your investigations?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is a standard thing because in order to be able to see exactly the centre of the impact and the damage on the asphalt indicating the direction from which the projectile came.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How exactly did you clean the area around the impact point?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: This place I cleaned -- I didn't have a broom or anything like that, so I used a cloth and I removed the material composed of different objects, tissue, blood, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could play on now from 02:38 until 03:30.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in general terms what kind of objects were on sale at Markale Market in February 1994?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Flour, oil, cigarettes, lighters, a lot of items that were used for different kind of gas installations. Very few sort -- types of fruit and vegetables were there. This is the kind of thing that was sold at the Markale Market at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask the technical booth to turn on the sound of the video for the next -- in fact for all of the videos we are going to play today. Now, I'd like to play the next 15 seconds and I'd like you to listen carefully to the voices, please, Mr. Besic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Stop it there, stopped at 3 minutes and 45 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you hear those voices, Mr. Besic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that one voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was the voice that you heard and who was that person?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: That was my voice because I was addressing the judge to permit us to begin the cleaning and freeing up of the material from the centre of explosion so that we could have a better view of the point of impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So is it right that you did not begin cleaning that location until the Judge gave you permission to do so?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: All the actions performed during an on-site investigation have to be done pursuant to the agreement and permission of the investigating judge. No act can be done without that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, just visible on the right-hand portion of the screen in front of you, one sees a pair of scissors. Do you have any idea why one might find scissors at that location?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: The scissors probably dropped from a market stall. All kinds of things were being sold at the market. People were offering anything in order to get a box of cigarettes, a litre of oil, sugar, flour in return, so among other objects the scissors were also there. They probably fell from one of the stalls, there's no other reason for them to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we now go to 6 minutes and 38 seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We haven't heard the translation of that voice asking for the permission, but I don't take it it's challenged by the Defence. We can carry on then on that basis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we can -- we'll start playing at 6:38.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Stop please at 6:42.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What do you see on the screen in front of you now, Mr. Besic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: You can see the point of impact there of the mortar projectile, the clearing has been done precisely in order to see the markings on the ground because they are used in order to determine the direction from which the projectile came. The sticks -- actually aids in the shape of the letter T were placed by the ballistics experts, and based on the damage of the asphalt surface they can determine the direction from where the projectile came.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is it correct that it was not part of your duties to determine the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: That is correct. This was something that was done by the ballistics experts. That was their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember who they were, the ballistics experts in this particular instance?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Mirza Sabljica, ballistics expert was there. And this other one, he died. I cannot remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. If we could now play from 08:37 to 08:47, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What -- stop it there. We stopped at 08:47. What do you see on the screen in front of you now, Mr. Besic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: This is the very centre of the explosion of the mortar projectile. You can see parts of the soil, the asphalt, pebbles that are in the centre itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could now play on until 09:20, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Stopped at just before 09:20.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe for the court what you saw in that portion of the video, please?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: In this part of the recording you can see the clearing of the very centre of the explosion. And after the asphalt, the pebbles, and the other material, the soil was removed, the stabiliser was found of the 120-millimetre mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did any members of the BiH MUP participate in removing the pebbles and removing the stabiliser?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: You can see from this that this was done by members of the UN, specifically from the FrenchBat. We didn't want to do anything until they came and saw for themselves and extracted the projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Why was it you didn't want to do anything until they came and saw for themselves?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: There were different kinds of speculations during previous shelling and when people were killed, so we decided that it was better that they do it rather than us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, after the members of FrenchBat removed the stabiliser, who did they give it to?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I took the stabiliser fin from the mortar shell and took it to the CSB crime lab as an exhibit, as evidence where it was properly recorded, packed, and kept or stored as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On the following day at what -- which is the 6th of February, 1994, what if anything happened to the stabiliser?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of February a team was formed for ballistics expertise which went to the scene again which was secured over a period of 24 hours, and my boss at that time Mohammed Hadzisakovic, went with the team as head of the criminal investigations. He took the fin with him to the location where the place was examined by ballistics experts, specifically Berko Zecevic, who actually compiled a report about this particular projectile and its impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to play on from the current location, to 09:20 until 09:39.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, where do you understand this footage has been taken?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: This was taken at the Kosevo hospital in the morgue. All the corpses were transferred to the morgue of the Kosevo hospital. We see a corpse here that is placed on a corrugated iron strip which had been on the roof of one of the stalls at the market, and people used it as a stretcher. They used the roof parts of the stalls as stretchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could just play another five seconds, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you see in that clip that there were several bodies which were lying on parts of roofing unit, if I may put it that way, which had been used as stretchers, it wasn't just one body?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see the corpses on several locations that are laid on the roofing pieces from the stalls. People used all kind of things to transport the wounded, the casualties, the dead, to the hospital as soon as possible and some to the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The video-clip stopped there at 10 minutes and 3 seconds. If we could now play from 19 minutes and 50 seconds until 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, we can see on the bottom left of the video picture, Mr. Besic, the date 6.2.1994, which was the day after the incident; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe what you saw in that portion of the video?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: At this place you can see the centre of impact. You can see the traces of damage on the asphalt surface, and the chalk marks the damaged parts. The chalk was put by the -- there by the experts who were doing the investigation at the scene. That is that ballistics part of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could move now, please, to 22 minutes and 20 seconds. If we could just play please from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Stop there, please, at 22 minutes and 28 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you happen to know what those markings on the ground refer to, Mr. Besic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I'm not an expert in that field, I wasn't there at the time, but the arrow indicates the direction of the north, 18 degrees. I don't know if that is the angle of impact or 18 degrees to the north-east. I cannot be sure but the arrow indicates the direction of the north and this degree, 18 degrees probably indicates the direction from where the projectile came.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we now play 26 minutes and 32 seconds to 26 minutes and 54 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe what you saw in that portion, Mr. Besic?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Again, this is the centre of impact of the explosion of the mortar projectile, and this was filmed by my colleague Suad Dzumisic, so this is a close-up and then probably from the roof of the building or from the building itself, there was another shot made of the wider area of impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And on the basis of those observations and on the basis of your experience in other investigations, does it appear to you that the projectile detonated upon impact with a roofing unit or upon impact with the ground?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: It's a fact that it came into contact with the asphalt surface, you can see damage on the asphalt surface. Had the contact been on the roof above this, the damage caused by the projectile, the centre, the stabiliser, would not be here. This location is therefore the very centre of impact of the mortar projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We are going to move now to the subject of photographs. Is it correct that you compiled a file of photo documentation relating to the Markale I incident?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I call up Exhibit P1709, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is this the -- on the left-hand part of the screen in front of you, is that the first page of the file of photo documentation which you prepared relating to the Markale I incident?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, I think it's fair to say, Mr. Besic, that this photo file is divided into three parts. The first part contains photographs of the incident location, the second part contains photographs of the stabiliser and of shrapnel, and the third part contains photographs of bodies of the deceased in a morgue; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you briefly clarify which parts of those you personally took photographs of?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I photographed the first photographs the way you divided them into three groups, I photograph the first group, the actual location. The second part was done by Suad Dzumisic in the lab, and he also did the photographs with the scale. The third photograph was done by Miralem Sarvan of the victims, and this was done in the morgue. This is a team. In view of the circumstances in which the whole event occurred, there were many wounded, so one team was at the location, one was working at the Kosevo hospital, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we move, please, to page 8 of the photo file, and could we blow up the photograph just so it's visible, and the text, to include the text below it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell the Court what this photograph depicts?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: As the caption says, it's the place of impact of the mortar projectile photographed after it was cleared from tissue and various items.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could go now, please, to page 12. This is photograph number 11 of the documentation file.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And just briefly describe what this photo shows?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: It shows again the centre of the explosion, and the caption says "after clearing of the debris in the place of impact of the mortar projectile, the stabiliser was found of a mortar projectile calibre 120 millimetres."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask the Registrar, please, to bring up page 4 of 65 ter 09620A.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: While that's coming, Mr. Besic, is it correct that yesterday you provided to me photographs which are essentially print-outs of the originals which you used to create this photo documentation file?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes. I brought it with me because we have saved the films. We have a video library of all the events filmed during the war and at any time we can make a still.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If I could ask the Registrar just to zoom in really on the centre of the photograph that Mr. Besic provided to us which is on the right. If I could just tell Your Honours that as you can see, the quality of the photographs Mr. Besic has provided, they are the same photographs, but we now have better quality images, so my suggestion, my submission is to upload those photographs which we've received and to associate them with this exhibit number so that Your Honours can inspect them, if you wish. The Defence have received copies of them. They are exactly the same photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there any objection from the Defence? That will be done, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll see to that. Thank you, Mr. President. If we could move on to the next photograph, please, in the photo file, which is photograph 12 on page 13. We can now close the other file.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just briefly tell us what this is, Mr. Besic.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: This is the tail-fin of the mortar projectile photographed after it was brought to the crime lab and photographed in black and white. You see a ruler on one side with dividers at intervals of 1 centimetres. This is always done with a photograph to determine the size.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we go to the next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What does this depict?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: It's the same projectile photographed from a different angle where you see the fuse itself and the markings on the fuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I now ask the Registrar to produce 65 ter 10457, please. This is the artifact, Mr. Registrar, you have in your custody. We can now show it to the witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Besic, are you in a position to identify that object?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the object.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: There was another band here with a marking that we make for our filing purposes, but it's missing here, but that's the object.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So just to clarify the record, is that the stabiliser from the Markale I incident?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Besic. We are now going to move to the Markale II incident. Now, you participated in that investigation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, sorry to interrupt you, but just for planning purpose, irrespective of our belated start, we are minded to take a break at 12.40. We'll have a break for half an hour, so you have ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. President. And I forgot, can I tender in evidence the Markale I stabiliser. This has already been admitted in evidence as part of the record in the Galic trial. I understand that the procedure here is that the same artifacts cannot be entered into evidence in two different trials, so I understand that we have to tender into evidence a photograph of the artifact. That's my understanding of the procedure. I'm open to correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's due to some administrative matters, reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I mean the Galic trial is completely finished, but I understand it still remains part of the evidentiary record in that trial. Certainly if it could be admitted in evidence in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, unless there's an objection we'll do so. We'll give this a number for...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P1967, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Photographs representing the real stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it's always possible to see the real artifact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, it will be in the custody the Registrar at all times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Besic, could you briefly describe your duties in the investigation of the Markale II incident?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Well, when that incident happened, the work of a scenes-of-crime officer consists of photographing the scene as found, video recording, photograph documentation, and collecting all the evidence that could be helpful in the investigation. In this case, a team was formed. We came out to the scene and we carried out that part of the work. As you can see from everything attached. If we hadn't done that job, there would be no photo documentation, there would be no sketch, there would be no projectile. At the end of the day, that's the point of police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is it correct that you personally took photographs of the location of the Markale II incident on the day of the incident?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did that and my colleague did the video recording. I made photographs and my colleague filmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can I ask for 65 ter 09533, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: To your right, Mr. Besic, you see a large whiteboard containing a composite of several photographs. Could you describe for the court what that depicts?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: This photograph was taken from the second floor of the building opposite Markale Market. It was a so-called panorama shot combined from four photographs. You see a lot of blood-stains, a lot of debris. You also see the centre of explosion of the mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Who took these photographs?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I did and I combined them to obtain this panoramic shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I tender that in evidence, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P1968, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm now going to play two different videos relating to this incident, and I'm going to begin with 65 ter 40102, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We stopped at 1 minute and 23 seconds. Mr. Besic, could you describe in general terms what that portion of the video shows?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: We saw a horrifying incident. You could see how many people fell victim, people were running to each other's aid. What can you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you specify which incident that was?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: That's the Markale II incident in Mustafe Baseskije Street, it is the northern entrance and exit to Markale.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could play now from 1 minute and 23 just to 1 minute and 26, just three seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you see in that clip a man moving a bicycle, Mr. Besic? We'll play it for you again if you wish.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes. That man is probably moving his bicycle to be able to extract a body because everyone is trying to help other people here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we play on, please, to 3 minutes and 20 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We can stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We stopped at 3 minutes and 25 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In that extract, Mr. Besic, you observed bodies of the deceased and injured being placed in vehicles; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court what kinds of vehicles were usually used to take away the injured and the deceased from shelling incidents on the basis of your experience?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: As we were all able to see, there's a Volkswagon Golf, there is a Jugo car produced locally. Cars of the newspaper in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was it the standard practice to leave the bodies of the deceased at an incident location or was it standard practice otherwise? By standard practice, I should say, the general situation in shelling incidents in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Well, wherever there were a large number of casualties, the first priority was to give assistance to people as soon as possible, to transfer them to the Kosevo hospital where they were met by doctors who did the triage, who sent those who were already dead on arrival to the mortuary, and helped the others. That was the standard practice in war time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. We can take a break now, if you wish, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take a break, about half an hour. We will resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I apologise yet again for the delay. There was some miscommunication amongst the Judges. So let's continue, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we play the remaining 35 seconds of the video that we were watching before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for purposes of planning, we'll sit until five to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about that portion, Mr. Besic. First of all, I think we saw, at one point, a soldier in that, and later on I'll show a video showing a couple of other soldiers. Did you personally go to the Markale Market very often in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes. A large number of people frequented Markale, without any distinction, in civilian, in military uniform. It was just a place for trading all sorts of goods. There were people in uniform as well as others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Court, on the basis of your observations, whether Markale Market was primarily frequented by civilians or primarily frequented by military personnel?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Well, it was intended for civilians. But in view of the situation in which the city was then, it was frequented by everyone, including people in uniform, and many people wore uniform. It was normally intended for civilians, but in those times people were wearing all sorts of things, whatever they could lay their hands on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to tender that video into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The whole of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, all of it. We've played all of it. The final portion we've played was from 3 minutes and 25 until 4 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1969, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to move to a video which has already been admitted in evidence as P1450, and I'll be playing some extracts from that. Initially, I'd like to play the first minute of this video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We've stopped at 48 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Besic, it's been repeatedly asserted in this court that many of the bodies at the Markale I and Markale II incidents were brought from the front-line, that the bodies were already dead. I want to ask you if you can comment on that assertion.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to comment. We can see, with our own eyes, everything that happened. All sorts of stories circulated, that bodies were brought there and planted there. However, we've seen what's going on. If dead bodies had been brought here, then the wounded people here would not be acting this way. You see the man without his lower leg. If you look at the other photographs and recordings, you will see parts of extremities. There were all sorts of stories and guesses, but the facts are here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you personally have any experience with the exchange of bodies which have been dead for some time?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes. We frequently worked in the mortuary of the Kosevo Hospital. All bodies received from exchanges had to be examined by the police, the police had to describe their condition, and those bodies received from exchanges and these bodies here are very, very different.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Explain, briefly, in what way they are very, very different.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: If we look at the photographs of the bodies in mortuaries, bodies brought from Markale I and Markale II, you will see that those are fresh bodies that have no soil on them, their skin is not puckered up, whereas the bodies received from exchanges are received in very bad condition, the skin puckered up, a lot of mud and soil on them, they are in sacks, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain approximately when you personally participated in the exchange of dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Well, the job of the police, with all the bodies received from exchanges at the Kosevo Hospital, was to send a team. Usually, my colleagues and I went. We would photograph, make records and documentation, and within a certain time the bodies had to be identified. That was done in 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, through to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to ask now if we can play from 1 minute and 30 seconds to 1 minute and 50 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Stop there, please. We're at 1 minute and 51 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain what building that is we see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: This entrance/exit on the north side to Markale, formerly Marsal Tita Street, now called Mula Mustafe Baseskije Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, simply to clarify and to orient the Court here, could you explain, where you say "that's the north side," that's the north side of what building, exactly?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the northern side of Markale, the entry/exit into Markale, and there is another southern entrance from Vase Miskina Street. That's the main entrance. This is one of the other entrances from Mula Mustafe Baseskije Street. There are another two side entrances, but they are not used.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The impact location for the Markale I incident, how far away was it from the impact location for the Markale II incident?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a distance of 100, 150 metres, not more, in the same street, Mula Mustafe Baseskije.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for clarification, the entrance that we are seeing is the entrance that is in that panoramic view, Mr. Besic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In respect of the picture on the screen in front of you, approximately where -- how far from the door was the impact location?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Looking from this angle, the point of impact is on the right-hand side some 4 to 5 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we play on now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, could you describe what we're seeing in this picture here?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Here we see one body in uniform. They are commenting that he is a soldier, he is probably a soldier who came there to buy something, or he was passing by and he got hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That was at 2 minutes and 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you at any stage encounter any information to suggest that any soldiers had been placed at the site?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: In that part of town around the market, there is no single location holding members of the armed forces. At least I'm not aware of any such location. Further away, there is the army hall, but it's some 500 metres away. And in this neighbourhood around Markale I and Markale II, there is no location holding BH Army members.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you encounter any information to suggest that any corpses of soldiers had been placed at this location?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can we play on now until 3 minutes and 7 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you confirm what door that is? That's at 3 minutes and 7 seconds.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Entrance/exit on the north side from the Mula Mustafe Baseskije Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like now to skip to 3 minutes and 40 seconds and play for 20 seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And stop, please. We stopped at 4 minutes and 2 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe what we saw in that extract?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: This is the situation as found when we came. There are members of the UN as well. Most of the location has already been cleared from people and from the wounded, and the place has already been secured by the police. And we proceeded to work to determine the facts of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you play on for 30 seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Stop there, please. Stopped at 4 minutes and 35 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Can you describe your understanding of what was going on in that clip?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: On this picture, we see that UN members are measuring the distance from the center of the explosion to the northern wall of the Markale Market, just close to the entrance. The white chalk marks the damage at the center of the explosion and damage incurred by shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to 6 minutes and 45 seconds. If we can play from there until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What did you understand to be taking place in that final clip?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: This is a list of the casualties in Kosevo Hospital. And this woman speaking was saying where each injured person was, most of them being in the Orthopaedics Department, which indicates that there were many injuries to the extremities in this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that ends the Markale II portion. I simply wish to clarify the photographs which you gave me yesterday. Is it correct that you gave me photographs relating to photo files from the Markale I incident, the Markale II incident, and the incident which took place in Dobrinja on the 4th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, the photographs we've received from Mr. Besic are some -- are most, but not all, of the photographs in those photo files relating to those three incidents, which have already been admitted in evidence, and we have up-loaded the photographs that we have. So I would just like to read into the record the 65 ter numbers pertaining to the higher-quality images which have been up-loaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In respect of P1709, which is the photo file for Markale I, the images received from Mr. Besic are at 65 ter 09620A. In respect of P1926, which is the photo file relating to Markale II, the photos received from Mr. Besic are at 65 ter 09900A. Finally, in respect of P1707, which is the photo documentation file relating to the Dobrinja incident, which is Incident G-7, the photographs received from Mr. Besic are at 65 ter 09624A. I'd like to deal now with the associated -- I'd like to tender those in evidence, and I'd also like to deal with the outstanding associated exhibits, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What do you mean by "tendering"? Do you like to replace the current pictures?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, no. The current pictures are in there. They are the official photo documentation files. These are simply high-resolution images of the same photographs, substantially.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, those three 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. They will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. 65 ter 09620A will be P1970. 65 ter 09900A will be P1971. And 65 ter 09624A will be P1972. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in respect of the balance of the associated exhibits, we pointed out, on the filing which we submitted for Mr. Besic on the 22nd October, I think it was, the exhibit numbers of those associated exhibits which have been admitted, and there are two further associated exhibits which have since been admitted since we made our filing. So I can weed out the ones which have not yet been admitted, or as Your Honours wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The ones -- the associated exhibits which have not yet been admitted are 09 -- 65 ter 09619, 10457, 10228, 09899, 10226 and 09910. So I would tender those to be admitted as associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We dealt with 10457 already. That's the real one?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That's correct. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Registry will assign exhibit numbers in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What about 9910? Oh, yes, you mentioned it at the end. I think that's consistent with what I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That ends the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor. Mr. Besic, you'll further be asked by Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Karadzic, let's begin your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Besic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would just briefly like to throw some light on the following. You started to work at the police in 1975?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 1st of March, 1975, and I have been working as a crime technician from 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Although we need to make a break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to say. Mr. Besic, because the question and answers should be interpreted into English, another official language of the United Nations -- of the Tribunal, so I would like you to put a pause between the question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 12 years that you worked there, what was the type of work that you were doing?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I continued to work at the police, but I worked in the Technical Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you became a crime technician and started to work in that branch, you processed crime scenes, was this homicide or something else?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: When I began to work in this field, I had to complete a six-month course first, which I completed. And then in 1988, I began to work actively on on-site investigations, and these were usually homicides, robberies, burglaries, traffic accidents, other types of crimes and incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how many homicides did you investigate before the war broke out? Before Markale, let's say. Before the war broke out, let's say.

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: During the four years, I conducted investigations into four homicides. There were very few cases at that time of homicide. And this required a more serious investigation, a more specific one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All of this was conducted as part of the investigation which was then done for a case which was brought to trial pursuant to provisions of the criminal law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in that sense, there were certain rules about the way the scene should be processed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back to Markale I. You took part in the on-scene investigation. Can you please tell us when you arrived at the market after the Markale I incident? When did you arrive at the market, and who came with you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: After the Markale I incident, after receiving information, in some 10 minutes the investigation team was formed, comprising the investigative judge, the technician, the policemen, and in some 15 or 14 minutes, we were there. By the time we got there, the scene was secured by policemen from the Stari Grad Police Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say "secured," what does that mean? What does it mean, to secure the scene?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: That means that the scene is secured from people entering and altering the scene in any way, the existing scene. This is something that was done by policemen from the Police Administration in Stari Grad. They did not allow any passersby or any civilians to enter the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that the incident occurred at 1220 hours, that the explosion occurred at 1220 hours? Let me help you. Let's look at 65 ter 09634, 09634. In the Serbian, this is page 5, and in the English, maybe it's page 4. In the first paragraph, we can see that the notification arrived at 1320 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says in the report, that the notification arrived at 1320 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at the report from the investigation. This is 9622, 65 ter 9622.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the report from the investigation, which states that from 1320 to 1600 hours, a criminal/technical examination of the site was conducted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think five minutes is the time -- is off here. The investigation began at 1330 hours, and it was completed at 1600 hours. In one place, also, it says that the explosion occurred at 1300 hours. So there is a little bit of a time difference here amounting to some five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You managed, in 10 minutes, to put together a team and to come to the scene of the incident; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: No. Actually, the team was formed and came to the scene in a period of 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at the last sentence of the first paragraph: "The projectile dropped around 1220 hours." You were informed at 1320 hours, and at 1330 you were already at the scene; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Isn't it a little bit unusual that you are informed about it a whole hour after the projectile dropped?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: We received the notification -- the Communication Centre was notified by radio that there was a projectile that landed, that a lot of people were wounded. A team is formed along the command -- chain of command, and a judge is appointed, and the team goes to the scene. In view of the type of incident that occurred, it's possible that there are some errors in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the previous document, it states that the notification arrived at 1320 hours, and then that you were at the scene already at 1330 hours. And it's not in dispute in any of the documents that the explosion, itself, occurred at 1220 hours. What happened during that hour before you were informed?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Since we are not all in one building, the prosecutors are in one building, the judges are in another, the police is in another location, we needed time to form the team, the duty prosecutor, duty investigating judge, operative workers, and that is exactly that amount of 40 minutes or so that we needed in order to form a team. Also, if the location is -- actually, in this case the location is some 500 to 700 metres away from where the police were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't see those 40 minutes. I see that the shell fell at 1220, that the information reached you at 1320, and that very quickly you came to the scene. It seems that you did not waste that much time. Someone else wasted an hour. And are you able, then, to tell us what happened to this time, what happened in that hour?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you take with you a photographer or a person who made the video-recording?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes. He's an integral part of the team. There is a crime technician that is in the team, a person who is a videographer, and other members of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many videographers did you take?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Just one, Suad --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have any other people who were video-recording at the scene?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell the name of the gentleman who took the video? The first name is Suad, and the interpreter couldn't hear his last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I mixed up Markale I and Markale II. It was Zlatan Sadikovic who was the one who was recording at Markale I.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For the transcript, can you spell the last name, Sadikovic, because the last name is not recorded correctly in the transcript. I think I spelled it -- did I spell the name correctly, this Sadikovic? Mr. Besic, I need your confirmation. Did I spell it correctly? Is the last name spelled correctly in the transcript now?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, Zlatan Sadikovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did Sadikovic, Zlatan, come with you, and was he a part of your official team, an official photographer?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was part of the team. At that time, he was working at the CSB, and he was working on developing films in our film lab. And he also was in charge of the video camera, and he would be present at certain on-site investigations to help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you take him with you?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a part of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you came to Markale, was the evacuation of those wounded and killed already completed?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, the scene was already free. All the wounded and the corpses had been taken away. There were no bodies. Only the extremities were left, tissue and blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is what this hour was spent on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Well, probably at the point of impact and explosion, you could see from the video footage the people going in and out of the scene, the kind of chaos, the vehicles coming -- arriving to take people away for treatment, so I don't know whether this was something that took 40 minutes or an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As a crime technician, did you have any problems with the fact that you were summoned only after the bodies were removed and the scene altered in a way that was not permissible under the law?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't really pay much attention to that. There was a large number of people and corpses. People needed treatment. This is not something that accords with the correct procedure according to the law, but this is a humanitarian act, a humanitarian issue, so I believe that that was how they should have done it. According to the law, the corpse should be left at the scene, if it's one corpse or two, but this is something that can be applied in peacetime. In wartime, the propositions change.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I to understand that the wounded were supposed to be taken care of immediately, but the dead should have stayed on the scene for purposes of crime scene investigation?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, in peacetime. But in wartime, humane considerations come first. This was something like a force majeure. Plus when something like that happens, there is no police on the spot. People need to be taken care of. People are more important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the first to come to the aid of the wounded and the dead at Markale I?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I was not at the scene, nor could I have been at the scene. Like everyone else, I saw it all from the videos and on television. I saw the people who came to help, people who were on the market, who happened to be on the market and were not injured. The same people who were on the market already came to the aid of others, those who were lucky enough not to be injured themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this work was mostly done by the soldiers and the policemen who were there?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: In my previous evidence, I said that it was a market open to everyone. It is not strictly for civilians or strictly for the army. Everyone frequents that market. As for the police, policemen are often present to prevent theft and such. And those members of the army who were there were probably off duty and came to the market to get cigarettes and swap goods, cigarettes for flour, or oil, or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the number of injured?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to say after all this time. The first figures were something like 60 people, but it turned out that there were 35, 40 in the mortuary, and the bodies -- and the injured [as interpreted] buried in numbers. I cannot say whether it's 58 or 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how many wounded; 200 something?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Approximately. Whether it's a little more or a little less, I did not find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And they were being aided by those who happened to be on the market and who were lucky enough, as you said, not to be wounded or killed?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Many people ran to them, perhaps out of curiosity, wishing to help. People who were passing by ran to the market after it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, in any case, there were many of those who were not hurt by shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, a certain number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are we then to conclude that there were between 400 and 500 people at the market?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's likely that there were many people there at that time. It's a very large surface. It's possible that there were 400, 500 people. The market can hold a thousand, perhaps. Yes, I would agree with 400, 500.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked, but never got the answer. Was there more than one cameraman?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: As far as the police is concerned, there was just one cameraman, Zlatan Sadikovic, and no one else. If there was anyone else filming, they could only have filmed from a distance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now play 65 ter 40125. It's an exhibit already, P1711, from 1 minute 05 to 1 minute 17, and later from 5 minutes 03 to 5 minutes 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what kind of goods were available at Markale attractive enough to draw 500 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see, there's a large variety of items, clothing, and everything else. If you think it was just a green market, selling fruits and vegetables, that's very far from reality. Each stall had something different. If you take the number of sellers and the number of people who came to trade and swap things, it could have easily been more than 500.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that we see on this footage that only one-fifth of the stalls, perhaps, hold something, and even that is very insignificant?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Play back to the previous image.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What could have possibly drawn 500 people to a market like this?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: What we see on the stalls now is the narrow circle of the explosion. The area to the side was not devastated, and the sellers who were there had probably picked up their goods in a hurry and left. That's why the stalls are empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you think the goods were collected and taken away before the wounded and the dead were helped?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Various people and passersby were helping the injured, and the sellers probably picked up their property and ran from the scene.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, we'll see a different film recording the evacuation, showing the market as empty as it looks on this image. Can we see 503 to 511? Oh, sorry, this is it. This has already been exhibited. Thank you. Could we now look at 65 ter 09513.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you make this sketch of this incident? 09513. Did you, Mr. Besic, make the sketch of the Markale I incident?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I can't say with any certainty that I worked on this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you switch into e-court from Sanction. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see that sketch here. Is this a drawing of the Markale Market, showing the dimensions of the main surface?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this layout of stalls, can you mark where the stalls actually holding any goods were?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I couldn't do that. I don't know how to mark, and more or less every stall or every other stall was occupied by a seller, by a vendor. I really cannot say. This shows the total number of stalls at the market. But how many goods there were, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can you mark the place of the incident? This, towards the bottom of the picture, is Mula Mustafe Baseskije Street?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's where the train line goes, and this is the place of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now tell us, where were these 300 people hurt by shrapnel scattered?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I can try, but the shrapnel is shrapnel. Shrapnel does not stay in the center of the explosion; it travels. It can hurt you at 50 metres distance. Most of the injured were in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I don't believe Mr. Karadzic has elicited evidence that 300 people were hurt by shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you give us the reference?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if 67 were dead and over 200 were injured, the figure comes close to 300. It's official information. That is the score of Markale I. Let us now look at G-8, 5th February. Sixty-six dead and over 140 injured, but some reports refer to over 200 injured and 68 dead from a mortar shell. This 120-millimetre shell killed 66 and killed at least 140. And according to other reports, there were 180 to 190 injured. That's the G-8 schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, did you mean the number or the way they were hurt?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I understood the question to refer to the number of persons injured by shrapnel, and I didn't -- I thought that was around 200. Now he's adding 200 to those who died to get 268.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So on that basis, we can carry on. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic? Do you remember the question or shall I ask the accused to repeat his question, Mr. Besic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember the question. I put a circle around an area that was very busy. Whether there were 200 or 260, it's hard to say. These were the first reports that were necessarily very terse. It was difficult to estimate the number of people injured. In the mortuary, we had at that time 35 to 40 bodies. The number of the injured, as reported, increased all the time. It's difficult to give precise figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the indictment is rather precise, and I'm now wondering about a couple of things. First of all, what were 500 people doing in an empty market? Second, taking into account all these stalls, where did they fit? Three, how did shrapnel reach so many people, with all these obstacles and stalls and bodies, because one body covers another? Can you, as a scenes-of-crime officer, explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not making a speech now. Ask questions one by one. What was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question was: What were 500 people doing in an empty market? My other question is: Where were these people standing who were hurt by shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Let the witness answer each question in turn, Dr. Karadzic. It doesn't help anybody to ask compound questions. Your first question that you were asked if you could answer it was: What were 500 people doing in what was said to have been an empty market? Can you help us on that, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we cannot assert with certainty that all the stalls were empty. That's one. People came out of curiosity, sometimes looking for just one thing. Whether they will find stalls full or bare, they don't know in advance. They came to the market to see what there was. I can't tell you what they were doing at the market. The second question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you are a scenes-of-crime officer and you know about these things. Taking into account all these stalls and all these obstacles, where did these 200 - some reports say 300 - people fit when they were hurt by shrapnel, mortally or otherwise? Where could they have possibly stood in this area to be reached by shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Well, the dead were probably close to the center of the explosion. And those injured were some 15 to 50 metres away, and, of course, they could be hurt by shrapnel, because it penetrates through tin, through plastic. They can easily be injured in the upper arms, the upper body. A shell is an explosive device created to kill, to kill the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: What I just used, to create -- to kill the enemy, that was the term we used in the JNA, when we served there, to kill enemy manpower. It has nothing to do with actual hostility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, those were hostilities, and not anymore. Now, who recorded -- who filmed before you came, before the evacuation was completed?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you. I was not there. I don't know who could have possibly done it. It could have been a wandering reporter. There were many journalists and even foreign reporters roaming the town, hunting for news. That was their job. It was a scoop to be the first on the scene of some incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that at the time, Radio Hayat was already operating?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: Yes, Radio Hayat was operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was a programme at this radio station where people could call in live during the programme. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: No, because the phone lines were not working. Definitely, I can really state that with certainty. In 1994, the telephones were not operating. I don't know how they could have been calling in live to a programme. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let me draw your attention -- let me carefully -- have you listened to this audio-recording that we're going to play? We don't have a transcript, so we would kindly ask you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like the witness to put his signature on this marked sketch and you tender it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Besic, would you kindly place the date and your initials on this sketch?

utterances.speaker: SEAD BESIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Number 1 is the center of the explosion. Number 2 is the concentration of the killed and those wounded. And the last question for today: This is a 40-second clip --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we have to rise. The Appeals Chamber will be here very soon, so we have to vacate as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the exhibit number for the marked map will be Exhibit D891. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn for today. We'll resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning. In the meantime, Mr. Besic, you are not supposed to discuss about your evidence with anybody else. We'll rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 9th day of December, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.57 p.m.,
